title: Putin Tells Iran's President Russia Will “Do Everything” to Help End Iran War
excerpt: Vladimir Putin met Masoud Pezeshkian in Turkmenistan ahead of the CIS summit, vowing Moscow would use its influence to help settle the months-long Middle East conflict.
body:
• Russian President Vladimir Putin met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian in Turkmenistan on October 8, ahead of Friday's Commonwealth of Independent States summit at the Caspian Sea resort of Avaza.
  • Putin said Russia is “ready to do everything that is in our power” to help bring an end to the Middle East war that began with US-Israeli attacks on Iran on February 28.
  • He credited Iran with making “real efforts” to end the conflict and noted the “positive evolution” of Moscow-Tehran relations.
  • Russia has announced no specific peace plan or timetable — the offer is diplomatic positioning for now, as Trump separately claims “productive discussions” with Tehran.

The meeting in Turkmenistan

Russian President Vladimir Putin told Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on Thursday that Moscow stands ready to help end the war in the Middle East, placing Russia more visibly at the center of diplomacy around the months-long conflict.

“We are ready to do everything that is in our power to contribute to the settlement of this situation,” Putin said, according to Russian state media, as the two leaders met in Turkmenistan ahead of a Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) summit that opens Friday in the Caspian resort town of Avaza.

“We are ready to do everything that is in our power to contribute to the settlement of this situation.”

— Vladimir Putin, meeting Masoud Pezeshkian in Turkmenistan

Putin added that Iran had made “real efforts to end the war” since the conflict began on February 28, when the United States and Israel launched attacks on Iran, according to Russian news agencies. He also pointed to “positive developments” in relations between the two countries.

An alliance deepened by sanctions

The optics of the meeting were as important as the words. Russia and Iran — two of the world's most heavily sanctioned nations — have significantly deepened their military and trade ties since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, becoming increasingly reliant on each other. Thursday's encounter, held on the sidelines of a gathering of former Soviet republics, underscored how that partnership has matured into open political coordination.

Moscow's alignment with Tehran over the war is explicit: Putin framed the conflict as one that had not begun through Iran's own actions, echoing the Kremlin's longstanding line. Russia has previously offered to help stabilize the Strait of Hormuz and the wider Gulf region — a strategically vital waterway that Iran continues to restrict as the conflict grinds on.

Why Moscow wants a seat at the table

Putin's offer arrives as diplomatic traffic around the conflict intensifies. Earlier this year, during a phone call with US President Donald Trump, Putin reportedly proposed that Russia take custody of Iran's enriched uranium as part of a broader deal to end the war — an offer Trump declined, telling Putin: “Before you help me, I want to end your war,” in reference to Ukraine.

Trump, meanwhile, has been touting what he calls “productive discussions” with Tehran, according to Fox News — suggesting parallel, competing mediation tracks between Washington and Moscow. Russia's repeated high-level contact with Pezeshkian signals that the Kremlin wants a guaranteed role in any eventual settlement, even as it maintains its strategic relationship with Tehran.

What to watch

For now, Russia's pledge remains diplomatic rather than operational: no peace plan, no timetable, and no announced mechanism for mediation. The substance will be tested at the CIS summit on Friday and in whether Moscow follows words with concrete proposals.

For Indian readers, the stakes are tangible even at a distance. The war has kept energy markets volatile and shipping through the Strait of Hormuz constrained for months — pressures that feed directly into fuel prices and inflation back home. A credible mediation track, whether Russian, American, or joint, would be the first sign in months that the conflict's economic drag on the region might finally ease.
